headline: Why Are the Fluke Leaving the Back Bays? Class Is in Session
subhead: Warm mud water is pushing the fluke program toward the inlet mouths while blues, weakfish, and kingfish fill in behind them.
body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a guy standing at the Brigantine ramp with a bucket of Gulp and a confused look on his face: "Darnell, why aren't they in the same spots as June?" Fair question. Let's take it apart the way I'd take apart a lesson plan.

Back in mid-July the sod banks off Absecon Inlet and up through the Reeds Bay complex were holding a nice fluke program — three-to-five-pound fish stacked on the current edges, feeding hard on the incoming as bait got funneled off the grass. That water has since climbed into the low-to-mid 70s on a sustained stretch of calm, sunny weather, and fluke don't love sitting in shallow mud once it gets that warm. We flagged this shift last week — said the back bay fluke would start transitioning toward the inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water pushed warmer, and that's exactly the pattern I'm seeing play out from Absecon down through Great Egg.

The better fluke this week are showing at the mouth of Absecon Inlet in 18 to 25 feet, tight to the rock piles on the Brigantine side, and along the deeper channel edge off Great Egg Inlet near the old range markers. Both spots are running cooler, cleaner water than the back bays because they're getting flushed twice a day by ocean exchange. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are the go-to, worked slow on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current is still strong enough to hold bottom contact but not ripping you into the rocks. I had a student — well, a former student, now grown and still fishing with me — put three keepers in the cooler off Great Egg Thursday morning doing exactly that, biggest going five and a half pounds. It's not a wide-open bite. You're covering ground and working the drift carefully, but the fish are there for anglers willing to hunt the structure instead of anchoring on memory from three weeks ago.

Striped bass are the quiet story right now, and if you're only fishing daylight hours you're going to think they've left the building. They haven't — they've gone nocturnal. With inshore water sitting in that same low-to-mid-70s range, the bass are avoiding the heat and feeding mostly after dark and in the gray light around dawn, holding on current breaks near the Ocean City inlet jetties and the deeper bends of Townsends Inlet. If you want a shot, fish the two hours either side of high tide at night with bunker chunks or a swimming plug worked slow along the rocks. Daytime bass fishing in the surf is mostly a bust right now, and I'd rather tell you that straight than send you out there disappointed.

Bluefish are about to become everybody's story. The blitz pattern that's been running hard on bunker schools up in Belmar and points north has been building steadily, and bait pods have been drifting south along the beachfront with the tide. We called this one too — said the blues would follow the bunker down the coast, and I'd expect that wave to reach the Atlantic City and Ocean City beachfronts within the next several days if this calm, stable weather pattern holds and doesn't scatter the schools. Keep an eye on the surf from the Ocean City boardwalk down toward Corson's Inlet — when the birds start working tight over a bait ball, that's your signal, and metal lures like a Hopkins or a 2-ounce Kastmaster thrown into the melee will get bit fast.

Weakfish are rebuilding on the evening tide, and this is a pattern worth being patient for. We noted last week that the weakfish bite should firm up on calm, warm evenings, and that's held true — the mouth of Great Egg Harbor and the deeper holes behind Ocean City have produced a scattering of quality weakfish in the last hour of light on the outgoing, fish in the 18-to-22-inch range hitting Storm Shads in root beer and pink worked slow near bottom. It's not the weakfish run of decades past, but for anyone who remembers what this fishery used to be, seeing legal fish show consistently on a July evening tide is worth noting.

On the sod banks — Brigantine marsh, the flats behind Longport, the grass edges up in Absecon Bay — kingfish and small blowfish have moved in, which is textbook July behavior in stable, warm shallow water. Bloodworms or small strips of squid on a high-low rig, fished on a light spinning outfit in two to four feet of water on a slack high, will keep a family entertained for an afternoon even when the bigger species are being stubborn.

Triggerfish are showing on the inlet jetty rocks and the nearshore reef structure off Ocean City and Sea Isle City, which happens every summer once the water settles into this warmer pattern. They're not a targeted fishery for most guys, but if you're bottom fishing sea bass structure with squid strips, don't be surprised when one of these odd, toothy customers shows up on the hook.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my daytime effort on fluke at the inlet mouths — Absecon and Great Egg both — while the back bay program keeps thinning out. If the calm weather holds through the week, I'd expect the bluefish blitz to arrive on our beaches by the weekend, and that's worth rearranging a Saturday morning around. Bass fishing stays a night game until we get a real cool-down. Class dismissed — go put in the work.
